text: A clean evolutionary question ("why green, not black?") won a category. Ask a why-question, then measure.
A computational project competed (and won) in Biochemistry. Category choice is strategic, not fixed.
One project, two major wins (ISEF category 1st + Google Science Fair Grand Prize).
In the first year CBIO existed, a two-person team shared 1st.
Top prize for a project where bioinformatic gene identification set up an engineering experiment.
Snails can win Animal Sciences Best of Category. Judges respond to applied invasive-species questions.
Public ENCODE/Hi-C data + a well-benchmarked predictor took CBIO Best of Category and STS top 10 in the same year.
A student who won a wet-lab category in 2016 came back and won CBIO Best of Category in 2018 with a network-biology method. Range across years is possible.
Public satellite data + simple, validated statistics went from an ISEF category 1st (2018) to STS 1st (2020). Simplicity with rigorous validation beats complexity.
Animal Sciences 1st for a citizen-science methods project. Judges valued making data collection scalable by non-experts, which is the premise of GBIF/iNaturalist-based work.
A methods-evaluation project ("which deconvolution methods work?") placed 2nd. Evaluating methods is legitimate science when done rigorously.
Google Earth Engine; supervised classification; correlation in R
Two-person CBIO team took 1st with public bioactivity data and a well-engineered GNN.
Global-scale analysis of public geospatial data took a category 1st as a two-person team.
Good pipeline, no award: public multi-omics -> network -> docking is now a common shape. Differentiate on the question and the validation, not the pipeline.
CNN on RGB/IR images; custom hardware
CBIO 1st and a $50k top award from public pharmacovigilance data: the hierarchy (reaction -> mechanism) gave it biological depth.
Public survey data + synthetic-data training + verified new discoveries. The discovery, not the model, carried it.
Back-to-back Animal Sciences 1st with a regression model, not deep learning. Appropriate statistics on real organisms is enough.
controlled colony experiments; multiple linear regression
GDSC/CCLE cell-line drug response (standard for this task)
Plain CV-on-organisms (plant disease from photos) can place 2nd in CBIO when the biological stakes are clear.
ISEF 3rd but STS 3rd ($150k): STS judges weight statistical depth and the student interview more than ISEF category judges.
public CF microbiome data + own assays
Computation that generates a hypothesis which is then tested at the bench is a recurring category-winning pattern.
CV on microscope images of a parasite egg won the $50k Moore Award. The images were the team's own, collected for a real screening need.
A pure sequence-model project (RNN codon optimization) earned a $50k award outside CBIO (Biomedical Engineering).
Wildlife conservation + CV + spatio-temporal modeling won a category and a top special award. Closest ISEF analog to a CV-on-animals conservation pipeline.
public land cover (NLCD) + CDC case data
A CBIO project on public pathogen genomes won a $50k top award. Timeliness plus a biological explanation of the data.
A three-person Animal Sciences team won $50k.
Back-to-back CBIO 1st with a pan-cancer public-genome analysis of one understudied variant class. Pick a neglected signal, go deep, come back next year.
Top award for a new algorithm on public data that produced a concrete discovery. Public data is fine when the method finds something new.
public cancer patient genetics + own experiments
Public cancer genetics + structure prediction + a wet-lab knockdown: the full "compute then validate" arc, rewarded at ISEF, STS and Davidson.
variant analysis; AlphaFold modeling; CRISPR; docking
An evolutionary lens on cancer biology won a category. Framing a genomics result as an evolutionary question is a differentiator.
CBIO 1st with public perturbation data: the win came from a clear methodology plus named compound predictions.
ML virtual screening on expression signatures
Public cancer-genome analysis with a defined mutational mechanism placed 2nd. Mechanism-first framing beats "we ran a pipeline".
Year 1 did not place. Year 3 was STS top 40. Non-placement is not a verdict on the idea.
"(Year 3)" in the title. Judges read multi-year depth as seriousness.
Multi-year field program with a computational add-on (photo severity scoring) kept paying out: ISEF Horvitz 2024, Davidson 2026.
plant pathology; field validation; image app
A two-person team won the $50k Moore Award.
Animal Sciences 1st + Scripps for a spatial ecology question with a mechanistic hypothesis. Spatial "where is the disease worse and why" framing is a winner.
field sampling; biochemical assays; spatial comparison
Animal Sciences 1st: a real organism-level experiment with AI analysis as the measurement tool. AI serves the biology, not the reverse.
public retinal image dataset + own cell models
Wet + dry hybrid: computation on a public image set, then validation in a second lab model. This "two independent lines of evidence" structure recurs among top winners.
in vitro models + ML on retinal images
A three-person public-data biomarker project took CBIO 1st. Teams win here when the biological claim is specific and defended.
CBIO 1st for a speech/health AI tool. The category is broad; "biology" includes human health signals.
Computational evolution of a virus from public sequence data placed 2nd two years running.
Iterating the same method across years moved him from 3rd to 2nd.
A three-person team won a top award. Teams are not penalized when each member can defend the whole project.
Same project won at JSHS (April) and ISEF (May). Stack competitions.
A pure modeling project on host–pathogen evolution took CBIO 1st. Computational Evolutionary Biology (EVO) is a live winning subcategory.
CBIO 1st in 2026: method integration (physics-informed + imaging) rather than a single off-the-shelf model.
Team CBIO projects can place 2nd. Sharma was also on the 2025 CBIO 1st team (KRT proteins in ALS).
Same project: ISEF CBIO 2nd (May 2026) and STS 5th ($90k, March 2026). One strong project, two fairs.
Instrument + AI + a real environmental measurement. Judges reward a complete pipeline that produces new data, not just a model on someone else's data.
holographic imaging; CNN classification; autonomous robot
Multi-year arc: Agrawal also placed 1st in EAEV at ISEF 2025 and 3rd at JSHS 2025 with related water work.
own histology images and field data
Animal Sciences 1st place went to CNN image analysis paired with real field trials. CV plus a biological experiment beats CV alone.
A rigorous computational-method project with no biology won the top prize. Method depth counts.
Markov chain Monte Carlo; computational geometry
STS 1st for a spatiotemporal model built on public weather and disease data. A computational-ecology/epidemiology project can win the whole competition.
remote sensing indices; regression; out-of-sample validation
$175k for reframing a known problem (screening) with a method from another field (IR). Cross-field method transfer is a recognized form of creativity.
CBIO top-10 at STS for an acoustic model of real hives. Organism-level field data + a validated model, no deep learning required.
STS 1st place was a computational biology method project. CBIO wins the whole thing when the method removes a real bottleneck.
CV classifier on photos of a rare disease placed 3rd. Hard-to-get, well-curated images plus a clinical need.
cancer cell-line metabolomics + expression (CCLE-type; not named in sources)
integrative analysis of metabolomic and transcriptomic profiles
Public archive + method + a released catalog others can use. "We produced a resource" is a top-prize shape.
Conservation ecology with a clear mechanism and a landscape-scale goal: $100k. Ecology does reach the STS top 5.
Public observational data + careful causal design placed 5th. Design quality, not data novelty.
STS top 6 for a statistics-first genomics method on public data. No deep learning, no wet lab: a well-posed Bayesian model was enough.
public sighting records + ocean circulation data
Public sighting records (observational, biased, long-term) analyzed with spatial statistics reached STS top 40. The design logic matches GBIF/iNaturalist work.
Three competitions, one arc: computational finding -> structural model -> knockdown -> drug screen.
STS 1st for a computational search that produced concrete new objects. "The program found 146 new X" is a sentence judges remember.
large public retinal image dataset + own cell models
Public-image AI + an independent wet-lab validation = $175k. The validation layer is what separates top-3 from top-40.
CNNs on retinal images; cell-model validation
comparative pharmacology in a non-model organism
public single-cell data + own cell model
Public data generated the hypothesis; two approved drugs tested in a dish confirmed it. Top-10 structure.
published cell-line cisplatin response (GDSC/CCLE-type) + patient tumor genomics (TCGA-type)
interpretable ML; transfer from cell lines to tumors
479 cancer cell lines (CCLE/DepMap-scale metabolomics + annotations) + own experiments
A 479-cell-line computational screen (DepMap/CCLE scale) with a wet-lab block as validation. Shows what judges want after the dependency analysis: one testable prediction, tested.
data integration workflow; pathway analysis; knockdown validation
